paper_context.research_question: How much quantitative benefit do word embeddings provide over traditional bag-of-words representations for document clustering, and how can this be measured using a nonparametric discrete-distribution (Wasserstein/EMD) clustering framework?
contribution_type: algorithmic application / engineering (scalable D2-clustering via recent optimal-transport solvers)
empirical evaluation (comparative experiments across datasets and embeddings)
tool/resource (code and preprocessed datasets released for reproducibility)
contribution_style: method adaptation/engineering (adoption and scaling of B-ADMM / OT barycenter methods within D2-clustering)
main_claims: A nonparametric D2-clustering approach that treats documents as discrete distributions over word-embedding space, using Wasserstein distance and efficient barycenter computation, is computationally feasible at scale using recent OT algorithms (e.g., modified B-ADMM / Sinkhorn-based advances).

The proposed D2-clustering method consistently outperforms a broad set of baseline document-clustering methods (TF-IDF variants, LSI, NMF, LDA, AvgDoc, Paragraph Vectors, spectral/Laplacian, LPP) across multiple datasets, especially on short-text datasets.

The framework provides a quantitative way to measure the gains conferred by word embeddings versus bag-of-words: in many cases pre-trained embeddings give significant improvement over random embeddings and bag-of-words, but embedding benefits vary by dataset/domain (e.g., limited gains on certain domain-specific corpora).

The method is relatively robust to the choice of general-purpose word embeddings (with some degradation for low-dimension or random embeddings) and less sensitive to its internal hyperparameter m (centroid support size) than to the number of clusters K.
The authors provide code and processed datasets enabling reproduction of reported experiments.
expected_evaluation_dimensions: Clustering quality on labeled datasets measured by ARI, AMI, V-measure and homogeneity/completeness
Comparative performance vs. a wide set of baseline methods across dataset types (short vs long texts, general vs domain-specific)
Scalability and runtime (time per iteration, parallelization, number of distance computations compared to baselines)
Sensitivity to word embedding choice (pre-trained vs random, embedding dimensionality)
Robustness to hyperparameters (support size m, number of clusters K) and initialization variance
Reproducibility (availability and completeness of code, data preprocessing, and experimental details)

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Documents can be represented as discrete empirical measures over pre-trained word embedding space with normalized term weights that meaningfully capture document semantics for clustering.
supporting_evidence: Sec.3.1 defines document dk as sum_{i=1}^{mk} w_i x_i where x_i are embedding vectors and weights w_i sum to 1.
Introduction motivates treating documents as point clouds in embedding space.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If embeddings or weighting scheme do not preserve semantic relations (e.g., domain-specific jargon missing from embeddings or inappropriate weighting), Wasserstein distances may not reflect meaningful document similarity, degrading clustering validity.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Squared Euclidean distance in embedding space is an appropriate transportation cost for computing Wasserstein distances between word vectors.
supporting_evidence: Distance cost C_{i,j} := ||x_i - x_j||_2^2 used in Eq.(2) and updated in Eq.(6).
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If embeddings are structured so Euclidean squared cost poorly models semantic dissimilarity (e.g., anisotropic or non-Euclidean geometry), EMD-based comparisons may be misleading and barycenters suboptimal.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Modified B-ADMM implementation (Ye et al., 2017) used here converges to adequate approximations of Wasserstein barycenters within reasonable iterations and tolerances for clustering purposes.
supporting_evidence: Sec.3.3 provides update rules and states variables converge to matching weights in Eq.(2).
Runtime section reports iteration counts (e.g., 36 iterations for Newsgroups) and termination based on label-change percentage.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If the solver converges slowly, stalls, or yields poor barycenter approximations, assignment updates and cluster means may be inaccurate, affecting both runtime and clustering quality.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript argues that treating documents as discrete empirical measures over word-embedding space and clustering them under Wasserstein (EMD) distance (D2-clustering) provides a principled, nonparametric way to quantify gains from word embeddings vs bag-of-words. It claims computational feasibility at scale by leveraging modern OT solvers (modified B-ADMM and related algorithms), superior clustering performance across many datasets (especially short texts), and robustness to embedding choices and centroid support size m; code is released. The logical chain is: (1) Embeddings map words to vector space -> documents become discrete measures (assumes this preserves semantics). (2) Wasserstein distance between such measures meaningfully captures document dissimilarity. (3) Clustering with Wasserstein barycenters (D2-clustering) yields high-quality clusters, but barycenter computation is expensive. (4) Recent OT algorithms (B-ADMM, Sinkhorn, etc.) make barycenter computations practical; with parallelization and pruning (Elkan), runtime is acceptable. (5) Empirical experiments on six datasets show D2-clustering often outperforms many baselines; sensitivity experiments compare pre-trained vs random embeddings and varying m, K. Strengths include principled model, leveraging recent OT advances, and broad empirical comparison. Weaknesses / breaks: scalability claims rest on parallel compute and selective runtime comparisons; baseline tuning and full experimental details (exact embeddings, seeds, hyperparameter grids, full numeric tables and statistical tests) are partially relegated to Appendix or omitted; some assumptions (Euclidean squared cost, adequacy of m, fairness of baseline implementations) are not fully tested. Overall, the argument is coherent and plausible but depends on reproducibility checks and additional sensitivity/statistical analyses to close several gaps where reasoning is currently inferential rather than fully demonstrated.

counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If pre-trained embeddings adequately cover domain vocabulary and semantics (A1 holds), then Wasserstein distances will reflect meaningful document similarity and D2-clustering should outperform bag-of-words.
If B-ADMM converges quickly with the chosen tolerances and vectorization (A3 holds), then computational cost per barycenter becomes acceptable and the method scales to the reported datasets.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper adapts modern optimal-transport solvers (modified B-ADMM and related OT methods) to implement D2-clustering that treats each document as an empirical discrete distribution over pre-trained word-embedding vectors. It frames clustering as iterative K-means–style assignment + Wasserstein barycenter updates. Main empirical claims are (1) computational feasibility at scale via vectorized/parallel B-ADMM and pruning, (2) consistent empirical superiority over many baselines (especially for short texts), (3) the framework can quantify gains from pre-trained embeddings vs random/bag-of-words, (4) relative robustness to embedding choice and centroid support size m, and (5) code/datasets are released for reproducibility. The manuscript reports runtimes on multi-CPU machines and selective computation statistics, presents comparative metrics (ARI/AMI/V-measure) and sensitivity checks (embedding dimensionality, random embeddings, m choices). specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper frames documents as discrete empirical measures over a word-embedding space and applies the Wasserstein (EMD) metric to measure inter-document discrepancy. To make EMD-based clustering practical, it adopts recent optimal-transport solvers (notably a modified Bregman ADMM algorithm related to Ye et al., 2017) to compute Wasserstein barycenters and implements a Lloyd/K-means-style D2-clustering loop: (1) assign documents to nearest barycenters via Wasserstein distances, (2) update barycenters by solving barycenter optimization via B-ADMM, and (3) repeat until convergence. Algorithmic engineering (vectorized updates, data-parallel synchronization for Eq.(5),(10), and Elkan-style pruning in assignment) is used to reduce the number of pairwise OT solves and make runs feasible on multi-core clusters. Empirically, the authors benchmark against many baselines (TF-IDF variants, LSI, LDA, NMF, Laplacian, LPP, AvgDoc, Paragraph Vectors) on six datasets (short, long, domain-specific), reporting clustering metrics (ARI, AMI, V-measure, homogeneity/completeness). Key empirical conclusions: D2-clustering often wins or is near-best, shows especially large advantages on short texts, provides a quantitative way to measure gains from pre-trained embeddings (vs random embeddings and bag-of-words), and is relatively robust to embedding choice and centroid support size m. The paper claims practical scalability (per-iteration times reported for Newsgroups and Reuters on 24–48 CPU cores) and a code/data release to enable reproduction. Overall, the contribution is incremental: it combines known conceptual ingredients (D2-clustering, OT barycenters, word embeddings) and modern solver advances to make a previously expensive approach practical for document clustering, and it offers a thorough empirical evaluation exploring sensitivity to embeddings and m. The novelty is primarily engineering + comprehensive empirical assessment rather than a fundamentally new theory or metric.

prior_stage_inputs: Shared extraction stage: claims C1–C5, assumptions A1–A9, runtime and experimental summaries, sensitivity analyses, code/data release statement, and retrievals for related OT and embedding works.
Manuscript sections: Introduction, Related Work, Sec.3 (Wasserstein + D2-clustering + B-ADMM), Sec.4 (Datasets, Methods, Runtime, Results, Sensitivity), Sec.5 (Discussion), Sec.6 (Conclusions).
specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The paper builds a coherent, minimally-assumptive pipeline to measure the added value of word embeddings for unsupervised document clustering. Core reasoning chain: represent each document as an empirical discrete distribution (weighted support points = word embedding vectors); use squared-Euclidean cost in embedding space to define 2nd-order Wasserstein (EMD) distances between documents; embed D2-clustering (a K-means-like alternating assignment + barycenter update) where cluster centroids are Wasserstein barycenters; adopt recent scalable OT solvers (modified Bregman ADMM and related vectorized/parallel routines) to make repeated barycenter computations tractable; optimize runtime using assignment pruning (Elkan-style) and parallel synchronization reductions; empirically compare against a wide collection of baselines (TF-IDF variants, LSI, NMF, LDA, AvgDoc, Paragraph Vectors, spectral/Laplacian, LPP) across six datasets (short, long, domain-specific); run sensitivity analyses varying embedding sources (pre-trained vs random, lower dimensionality) and centroid support size m; report that D2-clustering generally outperforms baselines (especially on short texts), that embedding benefits are measurable but dataset-dependent, and that code/data are released to enable reproduction. The paper's contribution is primarily an algorithmic application + engineering demonstration (scaling D2-clustering with modern OT solvers) together with an empirical benchmarking resource for quantifying embedding gains.
logical_argument_graph: P1: Word embeddings map words to a semantic vector space; documents can be viewed as empirical distributions over these vectors (A1).
P2: Wasserstein distance (EMD) between distributions naturally measures cross-term relationships between words; squared Euclidean cost in embedding space is used as transport cost (A2).

P3: Clustering documents by minimizing within-cluster Wasserstein variance requires computing Wasserstein barycenters repeatedly (D2-clustering objective), which historically was computationally prohibitive.
P4: Recent algorithmic advances (modified B-ADMM, Sinkhorn-like solvers) enable efficient approximate barycenter computation; vectorization and parallelization reduce wall-clock cost (C1).
P5: Implement a K-means-like D2-clustering using those solvers plus Elkan-style pruning to reduce pairwise Wasserstein computations and parallel sync minimization.
P6: Empirically evaluate D2-clustering vs broad baselines across heterogeneous datasets and embedding choices; compare using ARI/AMI/V-measure and homogeneity/completeness.
CONCLUSION A: D2-clustering is computationally feasible at scale with adequate hardware and outperforms a broad set of baselines, particularly on short texts (C1 & C2).

CONCLUSION B: The framework allows quantifying embedding benefit; pre-trained embeddings generally improve clustering quality over random/bag-of-words baselines, but gains are dataset-dependent (C3 & C4).
CONCLUSION C: Providing code and preprocessed datasets facilitates reproducibility, though some environmental and hyperparameter details are not fully documented (C5).

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: The manuscript proposes D2-clustering: represent documents as discrete empirical measures over word-embedding space and cluster them using 2nd-order Wasserstein (EMD) distance with K-means–style alternating assignment and Wasserstein barycenter updates. The practical barrier (costly barycenter computation) is addressed by adopting recent OT solver advances, primarily a modified Bregman ADMM implementation (Ye et al., 2017) with vectorized/parallel updates and Elkan-style pruning. Empirically, the authors compare D2-clustering against a broad set of baselines across six datasets (short/long/domain-specific), report clustering metrics (ARI/AMI/V-measure), sensitivity analyses (pre-trained vs random embeddings, lower-dimensional embeddings, centroid support size m), runtimes on multi-core CPU setups, and claim released code and preprocessed datasets. Evidence in the manuscript supports the core technical pipeline and some empirical wins (notably on short-text datasets) but several claims are partially supported or overstated given gaps: (1) scalability at "scale" is demonstrated only on multi-CPU clusters with selective runtime reporting and without full single-node/GPU baselines; (2) consistent superiority is shown but detailed numeric tables, variance estimates, and full baseline hyperparameter transparency are limited in the main text; (3) the claim that the framework 'quantitatively measures' embedding gains is supported by controlled comparisons (random vs pre-trained embeddings) but lacks statistical tests and rich provenance of embeddings. I flag methodological and reporting uncertainties, and enumerate actionable checks (reproducibility of runtime on different hardware, expanded sensitivity grids for m and embeddings, include mean/CI/ tests across seeds, and explicit repository URL/environment). I separate novelty-risk (few close precedents in documents applying full barycenter-based clustering at scale — innovation signal) from methodological concerns (operational dependence on high parallelism, assumptions about squared-Euclidean cost, pruning validity).

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: While prior works (Kusner et al. 2015) connect embeddings to EMD and Cuturi et al. and Benamou et al. supply barycenter algorithms, integrating modified B-ADMM into an end-to-end scalable D2-clustering pipeline for documents and providing broad empirical benchmarking is an engineering/empirical innovation. novelty_lenses.rationale: Combines known conceptual elements (represent documents as measures, Wasserstein distances, barycenters) with modern solver implementations and engineering (B-ADMM vectorization, pruning, parallelization) to make D2-clustering practical for document corpora — an incremental but valuable contribution.
evidence: Sec.3.3 Eqs.(5)-(13) and mention of Ye et al. (2017) software package
Empirical results showing practical runs on moderate-sized corpora

novelty_lenses.rationale: The work does not introduce fundamentally new mathematical formulations of transport or novel algorithms beyond adopting existing OT advances; its disruptive potential hinges on scalability and empirical superiority, which require stronger reproducibility evidence.
evidence: Key solver and algorithmic references are existing (Cuturi 2013/2014; Benamou 2015; Ye et al. 2017; Kusner 2015).
Manuscript frames the contribution as making D2-clustering practical rather than inventing new theory.

confidence_interval.rationale: Confidence reflects the manuscript's clear algorithmic pipeline and reported empirical wins (especially on short texts), but is tempered by incomplete reproducibility artifacts, limited statistical reporting, and dependence on multi-core hardware for scalability claims. consensus_findings: The paper presents a coherent, principled pipeline: represent documents as discrete empirical measures over word-embedding vectors and cluster them using a K-means-style procedure with Wasserstein (EMD) distances and Wasserstein barycenters.

Recent optimal-transport algorithmic advances (e.g., modified B-ADMM, Sinkhorn-family methods) are appropriately leveraged and plausibly make repeated barycenter computations far more tractable than older LP-based approaches.
Empirical experiments on multiple datasets show that the proposed D2-clustering often performs competitively and yields notable improvements on short-text datasets compared to many common baselines.

The authors performed sensitivity checks (pre-trained vs. random embeddings, reduced embedding dimensions, a few values of centroid support size m) and report that embedding benefits are dataset-dependent and that m has smaller apparent impact than K in their runs.
The manuscript claims a code and preprocessed data release to support reproducibility, and cites use of an existing software package (Ye et al., 2017) as the algorithmic backbone.
disagreements: Degree of novelty: Some reviewers view the contribution mainly as engineering/empirical (incremental but valuable integration of existing OT solvers into D2-clustering), while others see conceptual novelty in applying barycenter-based clustering systematically to document corpora; the disagreement centers on whether the assembly (engineering + broad benchmarking) constitutes substantial novelty beyond prior WMD/OT literature.

Strength and generality of the 'scalable at scale' claim: Reviewers agree the approach is tractable on moderately large corpora given substantial parallel resources, but disagree about how broadly that should be interpreted. One view interprets the reported multi-core runs as evidence of practicality; another treats those runs as indicating that substantial compute (24–48 CPU cores) is necessary, limiting broader applicability.

Interpretation of embedding gains: Reviewers agree pre-trained embeddings often help, especially on short texts, but disagree about how much of the observed improvement is attributable to embedding semantic content versus smoothing/sparsity effects or choices in preprocessing and baseline tuning. Some treat random-embedding baselines' partial competitiveness as a caution that gains may not be entirely semantic.

Adequacy of experimental reporting: Reviewers consistently flag missing details, but differ in severity assessment — some treat the omissions (Appendix, repository link) as fixable and not undermining core claims, others see them as material gaps that prevent confident validation of empirical superiority and scalability.
uncertainty_hotspots: Reproducibility of empirical superiority: missing explicit repository URL, pinned solver implementation versions, full hyperparameter grids and seeds for both the proposed method and baselines impede independent verification of reported metric advantages.

Scalability under constrained resources: reported per-iteration timings are on 24–48 CPU cores; single-node CPU/GPU feasibility, memory footprint, and end-to-end wall-clock comparisons to baselines are not provided.

Solver approximation quality: convergence diagnostics (primal/dual residuals, objective gaps) and sensitivity of clustering quality to B-ADMM solver hyperparameters (step sizes/tolerances, number of inner iterations) are not reported, leaving open whether barycenter approximations affect results.

Baseline tuning and fairness: baseline hyperparameter search procedures are referenced but not presented in the main text; fairness of baseline implementations (topic counts for LDA, rank/regularization for NMF/LSI, PV hyperparameters) remains uncertain.

Choice of transportation cost: squared-Euclidean ground cost is used without empirical evaluation against other potential costs (cosine-derived, Mahalanobis, learned metrics), creating risk that cost mismatch with embedding geometry affects clustering validity.

Effect and safety of Elkan-style pruning: adaptation of pruning to the Wasserstein metric and approximate barycenters is asserted to save computations, but its effect on assignments and final clustering quality (possible incorrect prunings) is not validated empirically in the paper.

These roles produce controlled disagreement about novelty significance while agreeing on empirical and engineering contributions.

Net effect: the reviewer ensemble combines tight logical scrutiny, rigorous reproducibility criteria, and graded novelty perspectives — this diversity reveals both practical strengths (sound pipeline, useful benchmark) and operational vulnerabilities (reporting, resource dependence).
meta_review.editor_guidance: The editor should centralize verification by requesting concrete reproducibility artifacts and focused validation experiments before relying on the comparative claims. Recommended prioritized actions to assign to authors or reviewers for rapid adjudication: (1) Provide a persistent public repository URL (or DOI) with pinned commits, a Docker/Conda environment, exact solver (Ye et al., 2017) commit hash or bundled code, scripts that reproduce at least one major table and figure, and random seeds. (2) Supply full experimental tables in the supplement showing mean ± std (or bootstrap CIs) across multiple runs for all methods and datasets, and report paired statistical tests comparing D2 to top baselines. (3) Deliver runtime reproducibility: run end-to-end timings (wall-clock) for at least one large dataset on a single high-memory CPU machine and, if feasible, a GPU node; supply memory usage and per-iteration counts. (4) Provide solver diagnostics: report convergence traces (objective values, primal/dual residuals) and ablate key B-ADMM hyperparameters to show stability of barycenter computation and insensitivity of final clustering to solver tolerances. (5) Validate pruning and cost choices: (a) show final clustering results with and without Elkan-style pruning for representative datasets to quantify any assignment differences; (b) run an ablation comparing squared-Euclidean to at least one alternate ground cost (e.g., 1 - cosine similarity mapped to a metric or a simple Mahalanobis scaling) and report effects. These focused checks will resolve the main uncertainties and allow the editor to weigh the empirical claims in light of reproducible evidence. Preserve the editor's central role by treating these verification items as gating information for interpretative weight rather than replacement of the editorial judgment.
meta_review.author_guidance: To strengthen the manuscript and address the reviewers' concerns, provide the following concrete materials and analyses: (1) Reproducibility package: public repo link with a clear README, Dockerfile or environment.yml, exact commit hashes of any external OT solver (Ye et al., 2017) used, scripts to reproduce main tables/figures, and random seeds for all randomized procedures. (2) Full experimental reporting: add supplementary tables listing mean ± std or bootstrap confidence intervals for ARI/AMI/V-measure etc. across multiple runs for every method/dataset; include paired statistical tests (Wilcoxon or bootstrap) comparing D2 to top baselines. (3) Baseline transparency: list hyperparameter grids, selection criteria, and exact preprocessing/tokenization/vocabulary choices used for each baseline; include scripts that run baseline tuning. (4) Scalability characterization: provide end-to-end wall-clock times and memory footprints for at least one large dataset on (a) single multi-core machine, (b) the multi-core cluster already used, and (c) optionally a GPU node; report per-iteration counts and number of inner barycenter iterations. (5) Solver diagnostics: include convergence traces (objective vs iteration), report primal/dual residuals or other diagnostics, and a small ablation showing how solver hyperparameters (step-size, tolerance, inner iteration count) affect both runtime and clustering metrics. (6) Ablations on cost and pruning: (a) compare squared-Euclidean cost with at least one alternative ground cost (cosine-derived or simple Mahalanobis) and report clustering impacts; (b) run and report cluster metrics with and without Elkan-style pruning to quantify any assignment differences and pruning safety. (7) Sensitivity sweeps: expand m and embedding-dimension grids (e.g., m in {10,20,50,100,200} and dims in {50,100,200,300}) and present performance/runtime trade-off plots. (8) Clarify code/data release scope in the paper (URL, license, included files) and ensure preprocessed datasets and scripts to reproduce preprocessing steps are included. Implementing these steps will materially reduce reproducibility and interpretability uncertainties and make empirical claims verifiable.

Consequently, some reported gaps (e.g., missing repository link, absent statistical tests) may be resolved in materials not included in the shared excerpts. human_facing_meta_review.summary: The manuscript adapts D2-clustering to text by representing documents as discrete empirical measures over word-embedding vectors and using 2nd-order Wasserstein (EMD) distances with barycenters computed via scalable OT solvers (modified B-ADMM and related techniques). Through engineering (vectorized updates, Elkan-style pruning, parallelization) and empirical benchmarking across six datasets and many baselines, the authors argue the approach is computationally feasible on multi-core hardware and often yields better clustering—notably for short texts—and that the framework can quantify gains from pre-trained embeddings versus random/bag-of-words baselines. Code and preprocessed datasets are reported to be released.
strengths: Principled representation: documents modeled as empirical distributions over embedding space, enabling cross-term comparisons without committing to single fixed-length vectors (Sec.3.1, Eq.1-2).

Algorithmic leverage: adoption of recent OT solver advances (modified B-ADMM, Cuturi/Sinkhorn literature) and vectorized barycenter updates to reduce per-barycenter cost (Sec.3.3; Ye et al., 2017 referenced).

Broad empirical scope: benchmarking against a wide set of baselines (TF-IDF variants, LSI, NMF, LDA, AvgDoc, Paragraph Vectors, spectral/LPP) on heterogeneous datasets (short/long/domain-specific) using ARI/AMI/V-measure and homogeneity/completeness (Sec.4).
Sensitivity analyses: experiments comparing pre-trained vs random embeddings and some variation of centroid support size m provide initial evidence on when embeddings help (Sec.4.5, Table 4).
limitations: Scalability claims tied to high-parallel resources: reported per-iteration runtimes (e.g., Newsgroups: 121s on 48 CPUs; Reuters: 190s on 24 CPUs) demonstrate feasibility only under substantial multicore hardware; single-node CPU/GPU performance, memory footprint and end-to-end wall-clock comparisons to baselines are not fully characterized (Sec.4.3).

Incomplete statistical and baseline-reporting: comparative claims are presented largely via summary figures/tables but lack consolidated mean ± std or bootstrap CIs across multiple seeds, paired statistical tests, and a transparent summary of each baseline's hyperparameter grids and tuning procedures (Appendix referenced but not included in excerpts).

Solver approximation and diagnostic gaps: the paper uses a modified B-ADMM solver (Ye et al., 2017) but does not report convergence diagnostics (primal/dual residuals, objective gaps) or ablate solver hyperparameters to show clustering robustness to approximation tolerances (Sec.3.3, Sec.4.3).

Ground-cost and pruning assumptions underexamined: squared-Euclidean ground cost is assumed without empirical comparison to alternatives (e.g., cosine-derived distances or Mahalanobis), and Elkan-style pruning is adapted to Wasserstein distances but empirical validation that pruning does not alter final assignments is not shown (A2, A9).
open_questions: Provide the exact public code/dataset link(s), pinned commit hash(es), and environment specification (Docker/conda requirements) so reviewers can reproduce at least one main table and figure. Where is the repository and what files are included?

Report full numeric tables (mean ± std or bootstrap CIs) across multiple independent runs for all methods/datasets, include the hyperparameter grids and selection criteria used for each baseline, and present paired statistical tests comparing D2 to top baselines. Can the authors add these to the supplement?

Supply solver diagnostics and ablations: what were the B-ADMM hyperparameters (step sizes, tolerances, inner iteration counts) per experiment, and how sensitive are ARI/AMI/V-measure results to these settings? Can convergence traces (objective vs iteration, residuals) be provided?

Quantify pruning and ground-cost choices: how much do final cluster assignments and metrics change when (a) Elkan-style pruning is disabled, and (b) the ground cost is replaced by a cosine-derived or simple Mahalanobis metric? Please provide comparative results on at least two representative datasets.
consensus_snapshot: Conceptually coherent pipeline: documents as empirical distributions over embeddings + Wasserstein distance + barycenter-based clustering is a principled framing.
Adoption of modern OT solvers makes repeated barycenter computations substantially more practical than older LP-based approaches, enabling experiments at nontrivial scale given sufficient hardware.
Empirical results indicate notable advantages for D2-clustering on short-text datasets and dataset-dependent gains from pre-trained embeddings versus random embeddings.
Reproducibility and robustness gaps (code/environment link, full statistical reporting, solver diagnostics, single-node scaling) are the principal unresolved items that limit interpretive certainty.
disagreement_snapshot: Novelty assessment: reviewers diverge on whether the contribution is primarily engineering/empirical integration of known OT techniques (incremental) or whether applying barycenter-based D2-clustering broadly to documents constitutes additional conceptual novelty.

Practical scalability interpretation: some treat the multi-core reported runs as sufficient evidence of 'scale' feasibility, while others see those results as indicating the method requires substantial compute and thus limited practicality without further optimization or GPU-based evaluation.

Attribution of embedding gains: reviewers agree embeddings help in many cases (esp. short texts) but disagree about how much of the observed gains are due to semantic content versus smoothing/sparsity effects or preprocessing choices and baseline tuning.
uncertainty_snapshot: Existence and completeness of the public code/data release (manuscript states release but explicit URL and content completeness are absent from provided excerpts).
Effect sizes' statistical significance: percent improvements vs random embeddings and baselines are reported, but uncertainty intervals and hypothesis tests are missing in main text excerpts.
Solver fidelity: unknown how barycenter approximation error from B-ADMM affects clustering quality across datasets and parameter settings.
Generality across hardware: unknown how broadly 'feasible at scale' generalizes to typical single-node or GPU-accelerated resources.

human_facing_meta_review.editor_guidance: Request that authors (1) supply a persistent public repository or DOI with pinned commits, Docker/conda environment, and example scripts reproducing one main table/figure; (2) add supplementary tables with mean ± std (or bootstrap CIs) across multiple runs for all methods/datasets plus paired statistical tests comparing D2 to top baselines; (3) provide end-to-end wall-clock timings and memory footprints for at least one large dataset on (a) single high-memory CPU, (b) the reported multi-core cluster, and (c) optionally a GPU node; (4) include solver diagnostics (objective traces, primal/dual residuals) and ablations for key B-ADMM hyperparameters; and (5) validate Elkan-style pruning and ground-cost choice by reporting results with/without pruning and with at least one alternative ground cost. Treat these items as verification steps that materially affect interpretive weight of comparative and scalability claims.
human_facing_meta_review.author_guidance: To address reviewers' concerns and strengthen empirical claims, provide: (1) a public repository link with README, pinned commit(s), a Dockerfile or environment.yml, and scripts to reproduce key figures/tables; (2) full experimental tables in the supplement reporting mean ± std or bootstrap CIs over multiple seeds and paired statistical tests (e.g., Wilcoxon or bootstrap) for D2 vs baselines; (3) explicit hyperparameter grids, selection criteria, and preprocessing scripts used for each baseline and for embedding preparation (model source, version, OOV handling); (4) end-to-end runtime and memory measurements for representative large datasets on single-node CPU, the multi-core cluster used, and (if available) a GPU; (5) solver diagnostics and an ablation showing sensitivity of clustering metrics to B-ADMM hyperparameters and inner iterations; (6) ablations showing clustering outputs with and without Elkan pruning and using at least one alternate ground cost (e.g., cosine-derived or simple Mahalanobis) on representative datasets; and (7) expanded sensitivity sweeps over centroid support size m and embedding dimensionality with runtime/quality trade-off plots. These additions will materially reduce reproducibility and interpretability gaps.
human_facing_meta_review.comments:
Summary: The paper develops a principled D2-clustering pipeline for documents by treating text as empirical measures over word embeddings and leveraging modern OT solvers (modified B-ADMM) plus engineering (vectorization, pruning, parallelization) to make barycenter-based clustering tractable. Empirical results across six datasets and many baselines indicate notable gains—especially for short texts—and experiments with random embeddings begin to quantify embedding benefits.

Strengths: Principled, assumption-light representation; effective use of recent OT algorithmic advances; broad empirical comparisons; initial sensitivity analyses exploring embedding vs random baselines and centroid support size m.

Limitations: (1) Scalability claims are demonstrated mainly on 24–48 CPU cores; single-node/GPU feasibility, memory usage and end-to-end timings versus baselines are not fully reported. (2) Comparative claims lack consolidated statistical reporting (means/stds, CIs, hypothesis tests) and clear, complete disclosure of baseline hyperparameter searches and preprocessing (Appendix referenced but not included). (3) Solver approximation diagnostics (convergence traces, residuals) and sensitivity to solver hyperparameters are not provided, leaving open whether barycenter approximation affects clustering outcomes. (4) The choice of squared-Euclidean ground cost and the safety/impact of Elkan-style pruning on final assignments are underexamined.

Open Questions: (1) Please provide the exact repository URL/DOI, pinned commit(s), and environment container or requirements to reproduce experiments. (2) Can you publish full tables with mean ± std (or bootstrap CIs) over multiple seeds and paired statistical tests comparing D2 to top baselines? (3) What B-ADMM hyperparameters (step-size, tolerances, inner iterations) were used per experiment, and can you provide solver convergence diagnostics and an ablation showing sensitivity of clustering metrics to these choices? (4) Please report results (assignments and metrics) with and without Elkan pruning and with at least one alternative ground cost (e.g., cosine-derived), on representative datasets.

Transparency: The manuscript cites and depends on Ye et al. (2017) for the barycenter solver and states code/data are released, but explicit repository links, pinned versions, seed lists, and detailed baseline hyperparameter tables are not included in the provided excerpts. Reported runtimes are explicitly tied to multi-core CPU counts; resource-dependence should be made explicit in the repository and supplement.

Epistemic limits: This synthesis is based on the portions and summaries provided (main text excerpts, shared analysis, specialist reviews) and did not inspect any external repository or the full appendix. Some of the reported gaps (e.g., repository link, appendix contents) may be resolved in materials not included here. Independent experimental verification will be required to fully substantiate comparative and scalability claims.

confidence_interval.rationale: Moderate confidence: conceptual framing and algorithmic feasibility are well-grounded in prior OT literature (Cuturi, Ye et al., Kusner) and the manuscript supplies concrete runtime and empirical summaries. However, incomplete access to full numerical tables, appendix hyperparameter details, pinned code/environment, solver diagnostics, and single-node/GPU scaling leaves substantial empirical uncertainty that reproduction and requested ablations could resolve.

Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Section: 1. Skim-reading: adjusting your expectations.
Codes: none
Applies To: claim_verifier, meta_reviewer, methodology_auditor, novelty_disruptive, novelty_incremental, structure_analyst
Content: What is the research question and what was done to answer it? Will the answer advance the field? Do NOT look at the results yet. Hindsight bias may make things seem obvious in retrospect, and confirmation bias may make you dismiss evidence that contradicts your beliefs. Remember that the goal of research is to contribute new knowledge. If the methodology and the type of contribution in scope of the CFP? NLP is an interdisciplinary field, and we might learn from papers that don’t do the same thing we do. E.g. there was a case when a *CL reviewer criticized a resource paper as follows: ‘the paper is mostly a description of the corpus and its collection and contains little scientific contribution’. This is particularly unfortunate when the modeling work has far outpaced the development of theory and documentation. Furthermore, given the sad state of replicability of NLP experiments, even in published papers, reimplementations and systematic analyses of prior work should be encouraged. Is the claim appropriately scoped? This applies to all papers, but especially to the short ones. They may present a proof of concept, an interesting finding, a convincing point, a negative result, and they are very easy to criticize with “it would be nice/more complete to add X”. Such a criticism can be made for most papers. It is only valid if the argument that is being made depends on X. In-depth reading. This is where you evaluate the evidence that is presented for its technical soundness, proof validity, sound argumentation, novelty, etc.

Section: Q: Why is peer review so inconsistent?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: much attention. In case of submissions that get deanonymized due to preprints and social media, we may also be biased in favor of well-known authors and/or widely-discussed papers. These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.
